title: Quantum simulation of non-Markovian dynamical systems
authors: Abtin Ameri, Arkopal Dutt, Hari Krovi
abstract: Existing quantum algorithms for simulating dynamical systems -- from Hamiltonian simulation to linear and nonlinear differential equations solvers -- simulate Markovian dynamics, in which the system's future evolution depends solely on its current state. We turn our attention to developing quantum algorithms for non-Markovian dynamical systems where the system's future evolution depends on its past history and thus has memory. Specifically, we develop efficient algorithms for linear Volterra integro-differential equations (VIDEs) with a convolution memory kernel that output a quantum state encoding the state description over a time interval or at a particular time. Given efficient circuits for the problem inputs, our algorithms achieve an exponential speedup in system size over existing classical algorithms.   We develop an algorithm for general kernels assuming that $\textsf{M} < 1$, where $\textsf{M}$ characterizes the strength of the memory term relative to the dissipation of the Markovian part of the dynamics. We complement this with lower bounds for general-kernel VIDEs when $\textsf{M} \geq 1$, showing that the problem becomes intractable for a family of systems. However, by specializing to structured kernels which admit concise decompositions over exponentials, we develop efficient quantum algorithms even when $\textsf M \geq 1$ by converting the VIDE into a larger set of ODEs, a procedure which we call Markovianization. As an application of the overall framework, we discuss the Mori-Zwanzig formalism used in open quantum systems and fluid dynamics. Overall, our results expand the range of dynamical systems that quantum computers can simulate efficiently.
summary: This paper tackles the challenge of simulating non-Markovian dynamics using quantum computation by developing algorithms for Volterra integro-differential equations (VIDEs). It achieves exponential speedup when memory effects are weak ($M < 1$) or when the system's kernel has a specific, structured form. This expands the scope of quantum simulation beyond traditional Markovian models into complex physical systems like those found in open quantum dynamics.
main_problem: Developing quantum algorithms capable of simulating non-Markovian dynamical systems, which retain memory of past system states.
main_result: Efficient quantum algorithms are developed for linear Volterra integro-differential equations (VIDEs) under specific conditions ($M < 1$ or structured kernels), achieving exponential speedup over classical methods in certain regimes.
method: The approach involves recasting the VIDE into a solvable linear system, utilizing Quantum Linear System Algorithms (QLSA) when memory effects are weak, or employing 'Markovianization' to convert the problem into an ODE set for structured kernels.
model_or_system: The focus is on linear Volterra integro-differential equations (VIDEs), which model non-Markovian dynamics where the evolution depends on a convolution memory kernel $K(t-	au)$. Applications include open quantum systems described by the Mori-Zwanzig formalism.
key_observables: Quantum state encoding of the system's state over a time interval or at a specific final time T.
important_parameters: The Memory Strength Parameter ($M$), which characterizes the ratio of memory term strength to Markovian dissipation; regimes include $M < 1$ (short-term memory) and $M \geq 1$.
main_assumptions: For general kernels, simulation is conjectured to be intractable when $M \geq 1$; efficiency for large $M$ relies on the kernel being decomposable as a sum of exponentials (SOE).
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the limitation of existing Markovian simulation algorithms, then develops efficient quantum circuits for VIDEs when $M < 1$, and finally introduces 'Markovianization' to extend this capability to structured kernels even when $M \geq 1$.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses simulating complex open quantum systems where memory effects are crucial, pushing the boundary of what quantum computers can simulate efficiently beyond simple Markovian master equations.
